idiom_name: Core Data entity inheritance (parent/sub-entity, one table per root hierarchy)
implementation_notes: Core Data models the hierarchy in the managed object model rather than in code: a sub-entity inherits its parent entity's attributes, relationships and model configuration, abstract entities are declared so they are never instantiated, and the store keeps every entity of a root hierarchy in one table with the type discriminator (the SQLite store's Z_ENT) - fetching Employee returns Employee objects while fetching Person returns all sub-entity rows. NSManagedObject/NSEntityDescription (or @Model in SwiftData) is the mapper layer, so the classic mapper class is replaced by the model plus fetch requests; the cost is the usual sparse table, which is why Apple's own docs and practitioners warn against factoring a couple of common columns into an abstract parent for large tables.
pitfalls: Every subtype attribute is an optional attribute on the single table, so 'required for this subtype' is enforced by your validation code, never by the model.
Raw SQLite access (or a batch update) bypasses the entity machinery and can leave Z_ENT inconsistent with the populated columns; keep such access read-only or re-derive the discriminator.

Changing the entity hierarchy (moving an attribute between entities, making an entity concrete/abstract) needs a model version and migration, and old stores keep rows whose type may no longer exist in the current model.

Factoring a couple of shared columns into an abstract parent puts unrelated entities into one table and is a known storage/performance anti-pattern unless the parent genuinely carries most of the state.
